entries.7e2e130d26f029339b4dd650b1a1f88df8a68c33: <div sID="gen2498" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Lev.19" sID="Lev.19"/> <div eID="gen2498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2499" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2500" type="x-p"/> Some ceremonial precepts there are in this chapter, but most of them are moral. One would wonder that when some of the lighter matters of the law are greatly enlarged upon (witness two long chapters concerning the leprosy) many of the weightier matters are put into a little compass: divers of the single verses of this chapter contain whole laws concerning judgment and mercy; for these are things which are manifest in every man's conscience; men's own thoughts are able to explain these, and to comment upon them. I. The laws of this chapter, which were peculiar to the Jews, are, 1. Concerning their peace-offerings, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.5-Lev.19.8">ver. 5-8</reference>. 2. Concerning the gleanings of their fields, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.9-Lev.19.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. 3. Against mixtures of their cattle, seed, and cloth, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.19">ver. 19</reference>. 4. Concerning their trees, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.23-Lev.19.25">ver. 23-25</reference>. 5. Against some superstitious usages, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.26-Lev.19.28">ver. 26-28</reference>. But, II. Most of these precepts are binding on us, for they are expositions of most of the ten commandments. 1. Here is the preface to the ten commandments, "I am the Lord," repeated fifteen times. 2. A sum of the ten commandments. All the first table in this, "Be you holy," <reference osisRef="Lev.19.2">ver. 2</reference>. All the second table in this, "Thou shalt love thy neighbour" (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">ver. 18</reference>), and an answer to the question, "Who is my neighbour?" <reference osisRef="Lev.19.33-Lev.19.34">ver. 33, 34</reference>. 3. Something of each commandment. (1.) The first commandment implied in that which is often repeated here, "I am your God." And here is a prohibition of enchantment (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.26">ver. 26</reference>) and witchcraft (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">ver. 31</reference>), which make a god of the devil. (2.) Idolatry, against the second commandment, is forbidden, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.4">ver. 4</reference>. (3.) Profanation of God's name, against the third, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.12">ver. 12</reference>. (4.) Sabbath-sanctification is pressed, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.3">ver. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.30">30</reference>. (5.) Children are required to honour their parents (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.3">ver. 3</reference>), and the aged, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.32">ver. 32</reference>. (6.) Hatred and revenge are here forbidden, against the sixth commandment, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17-Lev.19.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>. (7.) Adultery (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.20-Lev.19.22">ver. 20-22</reference>), and whoredom, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.29">ver. 29</reference>. (8.) Justice is here required in judgment (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.15">ver. 15</reference>), theft forbidden (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.11">ver. 11</reference>), fraud and withholding dues (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.13">ver. 13</reference>), and false weights, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.35-Lev.19.36">ver. 35, 36</reference>. (9.) Lying, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.11">ver. 11</reference>. Slandering, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.14">ver. 14</reference>. Tale-bearing, and false-witness bearing, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.16">ver. 16</reference>. (10.) The tenth commandment laying a restraint upon the heart, so does that (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">ver. 17</reference>), "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart." And here is a solemn charge to observe all these statutes, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.37">ver. 37</reference>. Now these are things which need not much help for the understanding of them, but require constant care and watchfulness for the observing of them. "A good understanding have all those that do these commandments."
entries.7ee9f65c31c0e21ff5f20c66f90582e402213886: <div eID="gen2500" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2499" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ceremonial and Moral Laws. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2501" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Speak unto all the congregation of the children of Israel, and say unto them, Ye shall be holy: for I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God <hi type="italic">am</hi> holy. 3 Ye shall fear every man his mother, and his father, and keep my sabbaths: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">4</hi> Turn ye not unto idols, nor make to yourselves molten gods: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">5</hi> And if ye offer a sacrifice of peace offerings unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , ye shall offer it at your own will. <hi type="super">6</hi> It shall be eaten the same day ye offer it, and on the morrow: and if ought remain until the third day, it shall be burnt in the fire. <hi type="super">7</hi> And if it be eaten at all on the third day, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> abominable; it shall not be accepted. <hi type="super">8</hi> Therefore <hi type="italic">every one</hi> that eateth it shall bear his iniquity, because he hath profaned the hallowed thing of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and that soul shall be cut off from among his people. <hi type="super">9</hi> And when ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest. <hi type="super">10</hi> And thou shalt not glean thy vineyard, neither shalt thou gather <hi type="italic">every</hi> grape of thy vineyard; thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <div eID="gen2501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2502" type="x-p"/> Moses is ordered to deliver the summary of the laws <hi type="italic">to all the congregation of the children of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.2">v. 2</reference>); not to Aaron and his sons only, but to all the people, for they were all concerned to know their duty. Even in the darker ages of the law, that religion could not be of God which boasted of ignorance as its mother. Moses must make known God's statutes to all the congregation, and proclaim them through the camp. These laws, it is probable, he delivered himself to as many of the people as could be within hearing at once, and so by degrees at several times to them all. Many of the precepts here given they had received before, but it was requisite that they should be repeated, that they might be remembered. Precept must be upon precept, and line upon line, and all little enough. In these verses, <div eID="gen2502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2503" type="x-p"/> I. It is required that Israel be a holy people, because the God of Israel is a holy God, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.2">v. 2</reference>. Their being distinguished from all other people by peculiar laws and customs was intended to teach them a real separation from the world and the flesh, and an entire devotedness to God. And this is now the law of Christ (the Lord bring every thought within us into obedience to it!) <hi type="italic">You shall be holy, for I am holy,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.15-1Pet.1.16">1 Pet. i. 15, 16</reference>. We are the followers of the holy Jesus, and therefore must be, according to our capacity, consecrated to God's honour, and conformed to his nature and will. Israel was sanctified by the types and shadows (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.8">ch. xx. 8</reference>), but we are <hi type="italic">sanctified by the truth,</hi> or substance of all those shadows, <reference osisRef="John.17.17">John xvii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit. ii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen2503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2504" type="x-p"/> II. That children be obedient to their parents: "<hi type="italic">You shall fear every man his mother and his father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.19.3">v. 3</reference>. 1. The fear here required is the same with the honour commanded by the fifth commandment; see <reference osisRef="Mal.1.6">Mal. i. 6</reference>. It includes inward reverence and esteem, outward expressions of respect, obedience to the lawful commands of parents, care and endeavour to please them and make them easy, and to avoid every thing that may offend and grieve them, and incur their displeasure. The Jewish doctors ask, "What is this fear that is owing to a father?" And they answer, "It is not to stand in his way nor to sit in his place, not to contradict what he says nor to carp at it, not to call him by his name, either living or dead, but 'My Father,' or 'Sir;' it is to provide for him if he be poor, and the like." 2. Children, when they grow up to be men, must not think themselves discharged from this duty: every man, though he be a wise man, and a great man, yet must reverence his parents, because they are his parents. 3. The mother is put first, which is not usual, to show that the duty is equally owing to both; if the mother survive the father, still she must be reverenced and obeyed. 4. It is added, <hi type="italic">and keep my sabbaths.</hi> If God provides by his law for the preserving of the honour of parents, parents must use their authority over their children for the preserving of the honour of God, particularly the honour of his sabbaths, the custody of which is very much committed to parents by the fourth commandment, <hi type="italic">Thou, and thy son, and thy daughter.</hi> The ruin of young people has often been observed to begin in the contempt of their parents and the profanation of the sabbath day. Fitly therefore are these two precepts here put together in the beginning of this abridgment of the statutes: "<hi type="italic">You shall fear, every man, his mother and his father, and keep my sabbaths.</hi> Those are hopeful children, and likely to do well, that make conscience of honouring their parents and keeping holy the sabbath day. 5. The reason added to both these precepts is, "<hi type="italic">I am the Lord your God;</hi> the Lord of the sabbath and the God of your parents." <div eID="gen2504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2505" type="x-p"/> III. That God only be worshipped, and not by images (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Turn you not to idols,</hi> to <hi type="italic">Elilim,</hi> to vanities, things of no power, no value, gods that are no gods. Turn not from the true God to false ones, from the mighty God to impotent ones, from the God that will make you holy and happy to those that will deceive you, debauch you, ruin you, and make you for ever miserable. Turn not your eye to them, much less your heart. <hi type="italic">Make not to yourselves gods,</hi> the creatures of your own fancy, nor think to worship the Creator by molten gods. You are the work of God's hands, be not so absurd as to worship gods <hi type="italic">the work of your own hands.</hi>" Molten gods are specified for the sake of the molten calf. <div eID="gen2505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2506" type="x-p"/> IV. That the sacrifices of their peace-offerings should always be offered, and eaten, according to the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.5-Lev.19.8">v. 5-8</reference>. There was some particular reason, it is likely, for the repetition of this law rather than any other relating to the sacrifices. The eating of the peace-offerings was the people's part, and was done from under the eye of the priests, and perhaps some of them had kept the cold meat of their peace-offerings, as they had done the manna (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.20">Exod. xvi. 20</reference>), longer than was appointed, which occasioned this caution; see the law itself before, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16-Lev.7.18">ch. vii. 16-18</reference>. God will have his own work done in his own time. Though the sacrifice was offered according to the law, if it was not eaten according to the law, it was not accepted. Though ministers do their part, what the better if people do not theirs? There is work to be done after our spiritual sacrifices, in a due improvement of them; and, if this be neglected, all is in vain. <div eID="gen2506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2507" type="x-p"/> V. That they should leave the gleanings of their harvest and vintage for the poor, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.9-Lev.19.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Note, Works of piety must be always attended with works of charity, according as our ability is. When they gathered in their corn, they must leave some standing in the corner of the field; the Jewish doctors say, "It should be a sixtieth part of the field;" and they must also leave the gleanings and the small clusters of their grapes, which at first were overlooked. This law, though not binding now in the letter of it, yet teaches us, 1. That we must not be covetous and griping, and greedy of every thing we can lay any claim to; nor insist upon our right in things small and trivial. 2. That we must be well pleased to see the poor supplied and refreshed with the fruit of our labours. We must not think every thing lost that goes beside ourselves, nor any thing wasted that goes to the poor. 3. That times of joy, such as harvest-time is, are proper times for charity; that, when we rejoice, the poor may rejoice with us, and when our hearts are blessing God their loins may bless us.
entries.5481ab6b3cd9915ca63bff01121f9517c48e3f9b: <div eID="gen2507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2508" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Ye shall not steal, neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another. <hi type="super">12</hi> And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob <hi type="italic">him</hi>: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning. <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind, but shalt fear thy God: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: <hi type="italic">but</hi> in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour. <hi type="super">16</hi> Thou shalt not go up and down <hi type="italic">as</hi> a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">17</hi> Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him. <hi type="super">18</hi> Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen2508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2509" type="x-p"/> We are taught here, <div eID="gen2509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2510" type="x-p"/> I. To be honest and true in all our dealings, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.11">v. 11</reference>. God, who has appointed every man's property by his providence, forbids by his law the invading of that appointment, either by downright theft, <hi type="italic">You shall not steal,</hi> or by fraudulent dealing, "You shall not cheat, or deal falsely." Whatever we have in the world, we must see to it that it be honestly come by, for we cannot be truly rich, nor long rich, with that which is not. The God of truth, who requires truth in the heart (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.6">Ps. li. 6</reference>), requires it also in the tongue: <hi type="italic">Neither lie one to another,</hi> either in bargaining or common converse. This is one of the laws of Christianity (<reference osisRef="Col.3.9">Col. iii. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lie not one to another.</hi> Those that do not speak truth do not deserve to be told truth; those that sin by lying justly suffer by it; therefore we are forbidden to <hi type="italic">lie one to another;</hi> for, if we lie to others, we teach them to lie to us. <div eID="gen2510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2511" type="x-p"/> II. To maintain a very reverent regard to the sacred name of God (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.12">v. 12</reference>), and not to call him to be witness either, 1. To a lie: <hi type="italic">You shall not swear falsely.</hi> It is bad to tell a lie, but it is much worse to swear it. Or, 2. To a trifle, and every impertinence: <hi type="italic">Neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God,</hi> by alienating it to any other purpose than that for which it is to be religiously used. <div eID="gen2511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2512" type="x-p"/> III. Neither to take nor keep any one's right from him, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.13">v. 13</reference>. We must not take that which is none of our own, either by fraud or robbery; nor detain that which belongs to another, particularly the <hi type="italic">wages of the hireling,</hi> let it not <hi type="italic">abide with thee all night.</hi> Let the day-labourer have his wages as soon as he has done his day's work, if he desire it. It is a great sin to deny the payment of it, nay, to defer it, to his damage, a sin that cries to heaven for vengeance, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jam. v. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen2512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2513" type="x-p"/> IV. To be particularly tender of the credit and safety of those that cannot help themselves, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.14">v. 14</reference>. 1. The credit of the deaf: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not curse the deaf;</hi> that is, not only those that are naturally deaf, that cannot hear at all, but also those that are absent, and at present out of hearing of the curse, and so cannot show their resentment, return the affront, nor right themselves, and those that are patient, that seem as if they heard not, and are not willing to take notice of it, as David, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.13">Ps. xxxviii. 13</reference>. Do not injure any because they are unwilling, or unable, to avenge themselves, for God sees and hears, though they do not. 2. The safety of the blind we must likewise be tender of, and not put a stumbling-block before them; for this is to add affliction to the afflicted, and to make God's providence a servant to our malice. This prohibition implies a precept to help the blind, and remove stumbling-blocks out of their way. The Jewish writers, thinking it impossible that any should be so barbarous as to put a <hi type="italic">stumbling-block in the way of the blind,</hi> understood it figuratively, that it forbids giving bad counsel to those that are simple and easily imposed upon, by which they may be led to do something to their own prejudice. We ought to take heed of doing any thing which may occasion our weak brother to fall, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.13">Rom. xiv. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.9">1 Cor. viii. 9</reference>. It is added, as a preservative from these sins, <hi type="italic">but fear thou God.</hi> "Thou dost not fear the deaf and blind, they cannot right themselves; but remember it is the glory of God to help the helpless, and he will plead their cause." Note, The fear of God will restrain us from doing that which will not expose us to men's resentments. <div eID="gen2513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2514" type="x-p"/> V. Judges and all in authority are here commanded to give verdict and judgment without partiality (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.15">v. 15</reference>); whether they were constituted judges by commission or made so in a particular case by the consent of both parties, as referees or arbitrators, they must do no wrong to either side, but, to the utmost of their skill, must go according to the rules of equity, having respect purely to the merits of the cause, and not to the characters of the person. Justice must never be perverted, either, 1. In pity to the poor: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not respect the person of the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.23.3">Exod. xxiii. 3</reference>. Whatever may be given to a poor man as an alms, yet let nothing be awarded him as his right but what he is legally entitled to, nor let his poverty excuse him from any just punishment for a fault. Or, 2. In veneration or fear of the mighty, in whose favour judges would be most frequently biased. The Jews say, "Judges were obliged by this law to be so impartial as not to let one of the contending parties sit while the other stood, nor permit one to say what he pleased and bid the other be short; see <reference osisRef="Jas.2.1-Jas.2.4">James ii. 1-4</reference>. <div eID="gen2514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2515" type="x-p"/> VI. We are all forbidden to do any thing injurious to our neighbour's good name (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.16">v. 16</reference>), either, 1. In common conversation: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not go up and down as a tale-bearer.</hi> It is as bad an office as a man can put himself into to be the publisher of every man's faults, divulging what was secret, aggravating crimes, and making the worst of every thing that was amiss, with design to blast and ruin men's reputation, and to sow discord among neighbours. The word used for a tale-bearer signifies a <hi type="italic">pedlar,</hi> or <hi type="italic">petty chapman,</hi> the interlopers of trade; for tale-bearers pick up ill-natured stories at one house and utter them at another, and commonly barter slanders by way of exchange. See this sin condemned, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.13">Prov. xi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.19">xx. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.4">Jer. ix. 4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.9">Ezek. xxii. 9</reference>. Or, 2, In witness-bearing: Neither <hi type="italic">shalt thou stand</hi> as a witness <hi type="italic">against the blood of thy neighbour,</hi> if his blood be innocent, nor join in confederacy with such bloody men as those described," <reference osisRef="Prov.1.11-Prov.1.12">Prov. i. 11, 12</reference>. The Jewish doctors put this further sense upon it: "Thou shalt not stand by and see thy brother in danger, but thou shalt come in to his relief and succour, though it be with the peril of thy own life or limb;" they add, "He that can by his testimony clear one that is accused is obliged by this law to do it;" see <reference osisRef="Prov.24.11-Prov.24.12">Prov. xxiv. 11, 12</reference>. <div eID="gen2515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2516" type="x-p"/> VII. We are commanded to rebuke our neighbour in love (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour.</hi> 1. Rather rebuke him than hate him for an injury done to thyself. If we apprehend that our neighbour has any way wronged us, we must not conceive a secret grudge against him, and estrange ourselves from him, speaking to him neither bad nor good, as the manner of some is, who have the art of concealing their displeasure till they have an opportunity of a full revenge (<reference osisRef="2Sam.13.22">2 Sam. xiii. 22</reference>); but we must rather give vent to our resentments with the meekness of wisdom, endeavour to convince our brother of the injury, reason the case fairly with him, and so put an end to the disgust conceived: this is the rule our Saviour gives in this case, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.3">Luke xvii. 3</reference>. 2. Therefore rebuke him for his sin against God, because thou lovest him; endeavour to bring him to repentance, that his sin may be pardoned, and he may turn from it, and it may not be suffered to lie upon him. Note, Friendly reproof is a duty we owe to one another, and we ought both to give it and take it in love. <hi type="italic">Let the righteous smite me, and it shall be a kindness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Ps. cxli. 5</reference>. Faithful and useful are those <hi type="italic">wounds of a friend,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.5-Prov.27.6">Prov. xxvii. 5, 6</reference>. It is here strictly commanded, "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt in any wise</hi> do it, and not omit it under any pretence." Consider, (1.) The guilt we incur by not reproving: it is construed here into a hating of our brother. We are ready to argue thus, "Such a one is a friend I love, therefore I will not make him uneasy by telling him of his faults;" but we should rather say, "therefore I will do him the kindness to tell him of them." Love covers sin from others, but not from the sinner himself. (2.) The mischief we do by not reproving: we <hi type="italic">suffer sin upon him.</hi> Must we help the ass of an enemy that has fallen under his burden, and shall we not help the soul of a friend? <reference osisRef="Exod.23.5">Exod. xxiii. 5</reference>. And by <hi type="italic">suffering sin upon him</hi> we are in danger of <hi type="italic">bearing sin for him,</hi> as the margin reads it. If we reprove not the <hi type="italic">unfruitful works of darkness,</hi> we have fellowship with them, and become accessaries <hi type="italic">ex post facto—after the fact,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Eph. v. 11</reference>. It is thy brother, thy neighbour, that is concerned; and he was a Cain that said, <hi type="italic">Am I my brother's keeper?</hi> <div eID="gen2516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2517" type="x-p"/> VIII. We are here required to put off all malice, and to put on brotherly love, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">v. 18</reference>. 1. We must be ill-affected to none: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge;</hi> to the same purport with that <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">v. 17</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart;</hi> for malice is murder begun. If our brother has done us an injury, we must not return it upon him, that is avenging; we must not upon every occasion upbraid him with it, that is bearing a grudge; but we must both forgive it and forget it, for thus we are forgiven of God. It is a most ill-natured thing, and the bane of friendship, to retain the resentment of affronts and injuries, and to let that <hi type="italic">word devour for ever.</hi> 2. We must be well-affected to all: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.</hi> We often wrong ourselves, but we soon forgive ourselves those wrongs, and they do not at all lessen our love to ourselves; and in like manner we should love our neighbour. Our Saviour has made this the second great commandment of the law (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.39">Matt. xxii. 39</reference>), and the apostle shows how it is the summary of all the laws of the second table, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.9-Rom.13.10">Rom. xiii. 9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.14">Gal. v. 14</reference>. We must love our neighbour as truly as we love ourselves, and without dissimulation; we must evidence our love to our neighbour in the same way as that by which we evidence our love to ourselves, preventing his hurt, and procuring his good, to the utmost of our power. We must do to our neighbour as we would be done to ourselves (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.12">Matt. vii. 12</reference>), putting <hi type="italic">our souls into his soul's stead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.16.4-Job.16.5">Job xvi. 4, 5</reference>. Nay, we must in many cases deny ourselves for the good of our neighbour, as Paul, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19">1 Cor. ix. 19</reference>, &c. Herein the gospel goes beyond even that excellent precept of the law; for Christ, by laying down his life for us, has taught us even to <hi type="italic">lay down our lives for the brethren,</hi> in some cases (<reference osisRef="1John.3.16">1 John iii. 16</reference>), and so to love our neighbour better than ourselves.
entries.a85ae2caff5801ea66abe8d1d1fa66c589071a8f: <div eID="gen2517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2518" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Ye shall keep my statutes. Thou shalt not let thy cattle gender with a diverse kind: thou shalt not sow thy field with mingled seed: neither shall a garment mingled of linen and woollen come upon thee. <hi type="super">20</hi> And whosoever lieth carnally with a woman, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> a bondmaid, betrothed to an husband, and not at all redeemed, nor freedom given her; she shall be scourged; they shall not be put to death, because she was not free. <hi type="super">21</hi> And he shall bring his trespass offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a ram for a trespass offering. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the priest shall make an atonement for him with the ram of the trespass offering before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for his sin which he hath done: and the sin which he hath done shall be forgiven him. <hi type="super">23</hi> And when ye shall come into the land, and shall have planted all manner of trees for food, then ye shall count the fruit thereof as uncircumcised: three years shall it be as uncircumcised unto you: it shall not be eaten of. <hi type="super">24</hi> But in the fourth year all the fruit thereof shall be holy to praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">withal.</hi> 25 And in the fifth year shall ye eat of the fruit thereof, that it may yield unto you the increase thereof: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">26</hi> Ye shall not eat <hi type="italic">any thing</hi> with the blood: neither shall ye use enchantment, nor observe times. <hi type="super">27</hi> Ye shall not round the corners of your heads, neither shalt thou mar the corners of thy beard. <hi type="super">28</hi> Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">29</hi> Do not prostitute thy daughter, to cause her to be a whore; lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness. <div eID="gen2518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2519" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A law against mixtures, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.19">v. 19</reference>. God in the beginning made the cattle <hi type="italic">after their kind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.25">Gen. i. 25</reference>), and we must acquiesce in the order of nature God hath established, believing that is best and sufficient, and not covet monsters. <hi type="italic">Add thou not unto his works, lest he reprove thee;</hi> for it is the excellency of the work of God that nothing can, without making it worse, be either put to it or taken from it, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>. As what God has joined we must not separate, so what he has separated we must not join. The sowing of mingled corn and the wearing of linsey-woolsey garments are forbidden, either as superstitious customs of the heathen or to intimate how careful they should be not to mingle themselves with the heathen nor to weave any of the usages of the Gentiles into God's ordinances. Ainsworth suggests that it was to lead Israel to the simplicity and sincerity of religion, and to all the parts and doctrines of the law and gospel in their distinct kinds. As faith is necessary, good works are necessary, but to mingle these together in the cause of our justification before God is forbidden, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.16">Gal. ii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen2519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2520" type="x-p"/> II. A law for punishing adultery committed with one that was a bondmaid that was espoused, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.20-Lev.19.22">v. 20-22</reference>. If she had not been espoused, the law appointed no punishment at all; being espoused, if she had not been a bondmaid, the punishment had been no less than death: but, being as yet a bondmaid (though before the completing of her espousals she must have been made free), the capital punishment is remitted, and they shall both be scourged; or, as some think, the woman only, and the man was to bring a sacrifice. It was for the honour of marriage, though but begun by betrothing, that the crime should be punished; but it was for the honour of freedom that it should not be punished as the debauching of a free woman was, so great was the difference then made between bond and free (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.30">Gal. iv. 30</reference>); but the gospel of Christ knows no such distinction, <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col. iii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen2520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2521" type="x-p"/> III. A law concerning fruit-trees, that for the first three years after they were planted, if they should happen to be so forward as to bear in that time, yet no use should be made of the fruit, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.23-Lev.19.25">v. 23-25</reference>. It was therefore the practice of the Jews to pluck off the fruit, as soon as they perceived it knit, from their young trees, as gardeners do sometimes, because their early bearing hinders their growing. If any did come to perfection, it was not to be used in the service either of God or man; but what they bore the fourth year was to be holy to the Lord, either given to the priests, or eaten before the Lord with joy, as their second tithe was, and thenceforward it was all their own. Now, 1. Some think this taught them not to follow the custom of the heathen, who, they say, consecrated the very first products of their fruit-trees to their idols, saying that otherwise all the fruits would be blasted. 2. This law in the case of fruit-trees seems to be parallel with that in the case of animals, that no creature should be accepted as an offering till it was past eight days old, nor till that day were children to be circumcised; see <reference osisRef="Lev.22.27">ch. xxii. 27</reference>. God would have the first-fruits of their trees, but, because for the first three years they were as inconsiderable as a lamb or a calf under eight days old, therefore God would not have them, for it is fit he should have every thing at its best; and yet he would not allow them to be used, because his first-fruits were not as yet offered: they must therefore be accounted as uncircumcised, that is, as an animal under eight days' old, not fit for any use. 3. We are hereby taught not to be over-hasty in catching at any comfort, but to be willing with patience to wait the time for the enjoyment of it, and particularly to acknowledge ourselves unworthy of the increase of the earth, our right to the fruits of which was forfeited by our first parents eating forbidden fruit, and we are restored to it only <hi type="italic">by the word of God and prayer,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.5">1 Tim. iv. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen2521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2522" type="x-p"/> IV. A law against the superstitious usages of the heathen, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.26-Lev.19.28">v. 26-28</reference>. 1. Eating upon the blood, as the Gentiles did, who gathered the blood of their sacrifices into a vessel for their demons (as they fancied) to drink, and then sat about it, eating the flesh themselves, signifying their communion with devils by their feasting with them. Let not this custom be used, for the blood of God's sacrifices was to be sprinkled on the altar, and then poured at the foot of it, and conveyed away. 2. Enchantment and divination, and a superstitious observation of the times, some days and hours lucky and others unlucky. Curious arts of this kind, it is likely, had been of late invented by the Egyptian priests, to amuse the people, and support their own credit. The Israelites had seen them practised, but must by no means imitate them. It would be unpardonable in those <hi type="italic">to whom were committed the oracles of God</hi> to ask counsel of the devil, and yet worse in Christians, to whom <hi type="italic">the Son of God is manifested,</hi> who has <hi type="italic">destroyed the works of the devil.</hi> For Christians to have their nativities cast, and their fortunes told them, to use spells and charms for the cure of diseases and the driving away of evil spirits, to be affected with the falling of the salt, a hare crossing the way, cross days, or the like, is an intolerable affront to the Lord Jesus, a support of paganism and idolatry, and a reproach both to themselves and to that worthy name by which they are called: and those must be grossly ignorant, both of the law and the gospel, that ask, "What harm is there in these things?" Is it no harm for those that have fellowship with Christ to have fellowship with devils, or to learn the ways of those that have? Surely <hi type="italic">we have not so learned Christ.</hi> 3. There was a superstition even in trimming themselves used by the heathen, which must not be imitated by the people of God: <hi type="italic">You shall not round the corners of your heads.</hi> Those that worshipped the hosts of heaven, in honour of them, cut their hair so as that their heads might resemble the celestial globe; but, as the custom was foolish itself, so, being done with respect to their false gods, it was idolatrous. 4. The rites and ceremonies by which they expressed their sorrow at their funerals must not be imitated, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.28">v. 28</reference>. They must not make cuts or prints in their flesh for the dead; for the heathen did so to pacify the infernal deities they dreamt of, and to render them propitious to their deceased friends. Christ by his sufferings has altered the property of death, and made it a true friend to every true Israelite; and now, as there needs nothing to make death propitious to us (for, if God be so, death is so of course), so we sorrow not as those that have no hope. Those whom the God of Israel had set apart for himself must not receive the image and superscription of these dunghill deities. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The prostituting of their daughters to uncleanness, which is here forbidden (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.29">v. 29</reference>), seems to have been practised by the heathen in their idolatrous worships, for with such abominations those unclean spirits which they worshipped were well pleased. And when lewdness obtained as a religious rite, and was committed in their temples, no marvel that the land became full of that wickedness, which, when it entered at the temple-doors, overspread the land like a mighty torrent, and bore down all the fences of virtue and modesty. The devil himself could not have brought such abominations into their lives if he had not first brought them into their worships. And justly were those given up to vile affections who forsook the holy God, and gave divine honours to impure spirits. Those that dishonour God are thus suffered to dishonour themselves and their families.
entries.330d774f371b3b1031f14ad54870071996a5f1c9: <div eID="gen2522" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Moral Laws. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2523" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> Ye shall keep my sabbaths, and reverence my sanctuary: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 31 Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">32</hi> Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 33 And if a stranger sojourn with thee in your land, ye shall not vex him. <hi type="super">34</hi> <hi type="italic">But</hi> the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">35</hi> Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure. <hi type="super">36</hi> Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">37</hi> Therefore shall ye observe all my statutes, and all my judgments, and do them: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen2523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2524" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A law for the preserving of the honour of the time and place appropriated to the service of God, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.30">v. 30</reference>. This would be a means to secure them both from the idolatries and superstitions of the heathen and from all immoralities in conversation. 1. Sabbaths must be religiously observed, and not those times mentioned (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.26">v. 26</reference>) to which the heathen had a superstitious regard. 2. The sanctuary must be reverenced: great care must be taken to approach the tabernacle with that purity and preparation which the law required, and to attend there with that humility, decency, and closeness of application which became them in the immediate presence of such an awful majesty. Though now there is no place holy by divine institution, as the tabernacle and temple then were, yet this law obliges us to respect the solemn assemblies of Christians for religious worship, as being held under a promise of Christ's special presence in them, and to carry ourselves with a due decorum while in those assemblies we attend the administration of holy ordinances, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1">Eccl. v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen2524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2525" type="x-p"/> II. A caution against all communion with witches, and those that were in league with familiar spirits: "<hi type="italic">Regard them not, seek not after them,</hi> be not in fear of any evil from them nor in hopes of any good from them. Regard not their threatenings, or promises, or predictions; seek not to them for discovery or advice, for, if you do, you are defiled by it, and rendered abominable both to God and your own consciences." This was the sin that completed Saul's wickedness, for which he was rejected of God, <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.13">1 Chron. x. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen2525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2526" type="x-p"/> III. A charge to young people to show respect to the aged: <hi type="italic">Thou shall rise up before the hoary head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.19.32">v. 32</reference>. Age is honourable, and he that is the Ancient of days requires that honour be paid to it. <hi type="italic">The hoary head is a crown of glory.</hi> Those whom God has honoured with the common blessing of long life we ought to honour with the distinguishing expressions of civility; and those who in age are wise and good are worthy of double honour: more respect is owing to such old men than merely to rise up before them; their credit and comfort must be carefully consulted, their experience and observations improved, and their counsels asked and hearkened to, <reference osisRef="Job.32.6-Job.32.7">Job xxxii. 6, 7</reference>. Some, by the old man whose face or presence is to be honoured, understand the elder in office, as by the hoary head the elder in age; both ought to be respected as fathers, and in the fear of God, who has put some of his honour upon both. Note, Religion teaches good manners, and obliges us to give honour to those to whom honour is due. It is an instance of great degeneracy and disorder in a land when <hi type="italic">the child behaves himself proudly against the ancient, and the base against the honourable,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.3.5">Isa. iii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.1 Job.30.12">Job xxx. 1, 12</reference>. It becomes the aged to receive this honour, and the younger to give it; for it is the ornament as well as duty of their youth to <hi type="italic">order themselves lowly and reverently to all their betters.</hi> <div eID="gen2526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2527" type="x-p"/> IV. A charge to the Israelites to be very tender of strangers, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.33-Lev.19.34">v. 33, 34</reference>. Both the law of God and his providence had vastly dignified Israel above any other people, yet they must not therefore think themselves authorized to trample upon all mankind but those of their own nation, and to insult them at their pleasure; no, "<hi type="italic">Thou shall not vex a stranger, but love him as thyself,</hi> and as one of thy own people." It is supposed that this stranger was not an idolater, but a worshipper of the God of Israel, though not circumcised, a proselyte of the gate at least, though not a proselyte of righteousness: if such a one sojourned among them, they must not vex him, nor oppress, nor over-reach him in a bargain, taking advantage of his ignorance of their laws and customs; they must reckon it as great a sin to cheat a stranger as to cheat an Israelite; "nay" (say the Jewish doctors) "they must not so much as upbraid him with his being a stranger, and his having been formerly an idolater." Strangers are God's particular care, as the widow and the fatherless are, because it is his honour to help the helpless, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.9">Ps. cxlvi. 9</reference>. It is therefore at our peril if we do them any wrong, or put any hardships upon them. Strangers shall be welcome to God's grace, and therefore we should do what we can to invite them to it, and to recommend religion to their good opinion. It argues a generous disposition, and a pious regard to God, as a common Father, to be kind to strangers; for those of different countries, customs, and languages, are all made of one blood. But here is a reason added peculiar to the Jews: "<hi type="italic">For you were strangers in the land of Egypt.</hi> God then favoured you, therefore do you now favour the strangers, and do to them as you then wished to be done to. You were strangers, and yet are now thus highly advanced; therefore you know not what these strangers may come to, whom you are apt to despise." <div eID="gen2527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2528" type="x-p"/> V. Justice in weights and measures is here commanded. That there should be no cheat in them, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.35">v. 35</reference>. That they should be very exact, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.36">v. 36</reference>. In weighing and measuring, we pretend a design to give all those their own whom we deal with; but, if the weights and measures be false, it is like a corruption in judgment, it cheats under colour of justice; and thus to deceive a man to his damage is worse than picking his pocket or robbing him on the highway. He that sells is bound to give the full of the commodity, and he that buys the full of the price agreed upon, which cannot be done without just balances, weights, and measures. <hi type="italic">Let no man go beyond or defraud his brother,</hi> for, though it be hidden from man, it will be found that <hi type="italic">God is the avenger of all such.</hi> <div eID="gen2528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2529" type="x-p"/> VI. The chapter concludes with a general command (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall observe all my statutes, and do them.</hi> Note, 1. We are not likely to do God's statutes, unless we observe them with great care and consideration. 2. Yet it is not enough barely to observe God's precepts, but we must make conscience of obeying them. What will it avail us to be critical in our notions, if we be not conscientious in our conversations? 3. An upright heart has respect to all God's commandments, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.6">Ps. cxix. 6</reference>. Though in many instances the hand fails in doing what should be done, yet the eye observes all God's statutes. We are not allowed to pick and choose our duty, but must aim at standing complete in all the will of God.  <chapter eID="Lev.19"/> <div eID="gen2529" type="x-p"/>

entries.5bebb2e3515da5b53bea755f16320cb1f18a5f49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1131"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.19.1-Lev.19.37">Le 19:1-37</reference>. A Repetition of Sundry Laws.</title> <div sID="gen1551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1131"/><hi type="bold">2. Speak unto all the congregation of the children of Israel--</hi>Many of the laws enumerated in this chapter had been previously announced. As they were, however, of a general application, not suited to particular classes, but to the nation at large, so Moses seems, according to divine instructions, to have rehearsed them, perhaps on different occasions and to successive divisions of the people, till "all the congregation of the children of Israel" were taught to know them. The will of God in the Old as well as the New Testament Church was not locked up in the repositories of an unknown tongue, but communicated plainly and openly to the people.<div eID="gen1551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ye shall be holy: for I ... am holy--</hi>Separated from the world, the people of God were required to be holy, for His character, His laws, and service were holy. (See <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.15">1Pe 1:15</reference>). <div eID="gen1552" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c056234290e48af88a53eb5d87a76097e66ccda: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1132"/><div sID="gen1553" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1132"/><hi type="bold">3. Ye shall fear every man his mother, and his father, and keep my sabbaths--</hi>The duty of obedience to parents is placed in connection with the proper observance of the Sabbaths, both of them lying at the foundation of practical religion. <div eID="gen1553" type="x-p"/>
entries.a328012977799328f8873ce2afe12acd8854b2d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1133"/><div sID="gen1554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1133"/><hi type="bold">5-8. if ye offer a sacrifice of peace offerings unto the Lord, ye shall offer it at your own will--</hi>Those which included thank offerings, or offerings made for vows, were always freewill offerings. Except the portions which, being waved and heaved, became the property of the priests (see <reference osisRef="Lev.3.1-Lev.3.17">Le 3:1-17</reference>), the rest of the victim was eaten by the offerer and his friend, under the following regulations, however, that, if thank offerings, they were to be eaten on the day of their presentation; and if a freewill offering, although it might be eaten on the second day, yet if any remained of it till the third day, it was to be burnt, or deep criminality was incurred by the person who then ventured to partake of it. The reason of this strict prohibition seems to have been to prevent any mysterious virtue being superstitiously attached to meat offered on the altar. <div eID="gen1554" type="x-p"/>
entries.e873eb694fa56498cf401d423c77dcf1baab981f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1134"/><div sID="gen1555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1134"/><hi type="bold">9-10. And when ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field--</hi>The right of the poor in Israel to glean after reapers, as well as to the unreaped corners of the field, was secured by a positive statute; and this, in addition to other enactments connected with the ceremonial law, formed a beneficial provision for their support. At the same time, proprietors were not obliged to admit them into the field until the grain had been carried off the field; and they seem also to have been left at liberty to choose the poor whom they deemed the most deserving or needful (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.2">Ru 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>). This was the earliest law for the benefit of the poor that we read of in the code of any people; and it combined in admirable union the obligation of a public duty with the exercise of private and voluntary benevolence at a time when the hearts of the rich would be strongly inclined to liberality. <div eID="gen1555" type="x-p"/>
entries.37f60db5e46c32af538ce1506308a3742a646ed6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1135"/><div sID="gen1556" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1135"/><hi type="bold">11-16. Ye shall not steal--</hi>A variety of social duties are inculcated in this passage, chiefly in reference to common and little-thought-of vices to which mankind are exceedingly prone; such as committing petty frauds, or not scrupling to violate truth in transactions of business, ridiculing bodily infirmities, or circulating stories to the prejudice of others. In opposition to these bad habits, a spirit of humanity and brotherly kindness is strongly enforced. <div eID="gen1556" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f245cdde2f5f3ef291789dc61f5e1309a5d99df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1136"/><div sID="gen1557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1136"/><hi type="bold">17. thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour--</hi>Instead of cherishing latent feelings of malice or meditating purposes of revenge against a person who has committed an insult or injury against them, God's people were taught to remonstrate with the offender and endeavor, by calm and kindly reason, to bring him to a sense of his fault.<div eID="gen1557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not suffer sin upon him--</hi>literally, "that ye may not participate in his sin." <div eID="gen1558" type="x-p"/>
entries.78f2d5a686dfc83c0f2ba3d6d6c0672eee46aa15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1137"/><div sID="gen1559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1137"/><hi type="bold">18. thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself--</hi>The word "neighbour" is used as synonymous with "fellow creature." The Israelites in a later age restricted its meaning as applicable only to their own countrymen. This narrow interpretation was refuted by our Lord in a beautiful parable (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.30-Luke.10.37">Lu 10:30-37</reference>). <div eID="gen1559" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b190827402c80c44dcb7783b373734178a57f35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1138"/><div sID="gen1560" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1138"/><hi type="bold">19. Thou shalt not let thy cattle gender with a diverse kind--</hi>This prohibition was probably intended to discourage a practice which seemed to infringe upon the economy which God has established in the animal kingdom.<div eID="gen1560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1561" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt not sow thy field with mingled seed--</hi>This also was directed against an idolatrous practice, namely, that of the ancient Zabians, or fire-worshippers, who sowed different seeds, accompanying the act with magical rites and invocations; and commentators have generally thought the design of this and the preceding law was to put an end to the unnatural lusts and foolish superstitions which were prevalent among the heathen. But the reason of the prohibition was probably deeper: for those who have studied the diseases of land and vegetables tell us, that the practice of mingling seeds is injurious both to flowers and to grains. "If the various genera of the natural order Gramineæ, which includes the grains and the grasses, should be sown in the same field, and flower at the same time, so that the pollen of the two flowers mix, a spurious seed will be the consequence, called by the farmers chess. It is always inferior and unlike either of the two grains that produced it, in size, flavor, and nutritious principles. Independently of contributing to disease the soil, they never fail to produce the same in animals and men that feed on them" [Whitlaw].<div eID="gen1561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither shall a garment mingled of linen and woollen come upon thee--</hi>Although this precept, like the other two with which it is associated, was in all probability designed to root out some superstition, it seems to have had a further meaning. The law, it is to be observed, did not prohibit the Israelites wearing many different kinds of cloths together, but only the two specified; and the observations and researches of modern science have proved that "wool, when combined with linen, increases its power of passing off the electricity from the body. In hot climates, it brings on malignant fevers and exhausts the strength; and when passing off from the body, it meets with the heated air, inflames and excoriates like a blister" [Whitlaw]. (See <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.17">Eze 44:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen1562" type="x-p"/>
entries.696754768f1d3d4f4e935558867097a607b0307f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1139"/><div sID="gen1563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1139"/><hi type="bold">23-25. ye shall count the fruit thereof as uncircumcised; three years ... it shall not be eaten of--</hi>"The wisdom of this law is very striking. Every gardener will teach us not to let fruit trees bear in their earliest years, but to pluck off the blossoms: and for this reason, that they will thus thrive the better, and bear more abundantly afterwards. The very expression, 'to regard them as uncircumcised,' suggests the propriety of pinching them off; I do not say cutting them off, because it is generally the hand, and not a knife, that is employed in this operation" [Michaelis]. <div eID="gen1563" type="x-p"/>
entries.018ca3095ace5e2813e02f34065d37a834164f23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1140"/><div sID="gen1564" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1140"/><hi type="bold">26. shall not eat any thing with the blood--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Lev.17.10">Le 17:10</reference>).<div eID="gen1564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... use enchantment, nor observe times--</hi>The former refers to divination by serpents--one of the earliest forms of enchantment, and the other means the observation, literally, of clouds, as a study of the appearance and motion of clouds was a common way of foretelling good or bad fortune. Such absurd but deep-rooted superstitions often put a stop to the prosecution of serious and important transactions, but they were forbidden especially as implying a want of faith in the being, or of reliance on the providence of God. <div eID="gen1565" type="x-p"/>
entries.69f9a93a6c726947aa9a91b5242e472924f651d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1141"/><div sID="gen1566" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1141"/><hi type="bold">27. Ye shall not round the corners of your heads, &c.--</hi>It seems probable that this fashion had been learned by the Israelites in Egypt, for the ancient Egyptians had their dark locks cropped short or shaved with great nicety, so that what remained on the crown appeared in the form of a circle surrounding the head, while the beard was dressed into a square form. This kind of coiffure had a highly idolatrous meaning; and it was adopted, with some slight variations, by almost all idolaters in ancient times. (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.25">Jr 9:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.23">25:23</reference>, where "in the utmost corners" means having the corners of their hair cut.) Frequently a lock or tuft of hair was left on the hinder part of the head, the rest being cut round in the form of a ring, as the Turks, Chinese, and Hindus do at the present day.<div eID="gen1566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither shalt thou mar, &c.--</hi>The Egyptians used to cut or shave off their whiskers, as may be seen in the coffins of mummies, and the representations of divinities on the monuments. But the Hebrews, in order to separate them from the neighboring nations, or perhaps to put a stop to some existing superstition, were forbidden to imitate this practice. It may appear surprising that Moses should condescend to such minutiæ as that of regulating the fashion of the hair and the beard--matters which do not usually occupy the attention of a legislator--and which appear widely remote from the province either of government or of a religion. A strong presumption, therefore, arises that he had in mind by these regulations to combat some superstitious practices of the Egyptians. <div eID="gen1567" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5f0cd9d1b1ac8d7df34340fc8edae623b45c8bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1142"/><div sID="gen1568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1142"/><hi type="bold">28. Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead--</hi>The practice of making deep gashes on the face and arms and legs, in time of bereavement, was universal among the heathen, and it was deemed a becoming mark of respect for the dead, as well as a sort of propitiatory offering to the deities who presided over death and the grave. The Jews learned this custom in Egypt, and though weaned from it, relapsed in a later and degenerate age into this old superstition (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Is 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.6">Jr 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.5">41:5</reference>).<div eID="gen1568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1569" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor print any marks upon you--</hi>by tattooing, imprinting figures of flowers, leaves, stars, and other fanciful devices on various parts of their person. The impression was made sometimes by means of a hot iron, sometimes by ink or paint, as is done by the Arab females of the present day and the different castes of the Hindus. It is probable that a strong propensity to adopt such marks in honor of some idol gave occasion to the prohibition in this verse; and they were wisely forbidden, for they were signs of apostasy; and, when once made, they were insuperable obstacles to a return. (See allusions to the practice, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Is 44:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.17">Re 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.1">14:1</reference>). <div eID="gen1569" type="x-p"/>
entries.66c56ec9bdad96bbc3aee5363331495695fbf531: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1143"/><div sID="gen1570" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1143"/><hi type="bold">30. Ye shall keep my sabbaths, and reverence my sanctuary--</hi>This precept is frequently repeated along with the prohibition of idolatrous practices, and here it stands closely connected with the superstitions forbidden in the previous verses. <div eID="gen1570" type="x-p"/>
entries.783ee8587681b7cfe5a5ce9170c605b0fcfe8473: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1144"/><div sID="gen1571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1144"/><hi type="bold">31. Regard not them that have familiar spirits--</hi>The Hebrew word, rendered "familiar spirit," signifies the belly, and sometimes a leathern bottle, from its similarity to the belly. It was applied in the sense of this passage to ventriloquists, who pretended to have communication with the invisible world. The Hebrews were strictly forbidden to consult them as the vain but high pretensions of those impostors were derogatory to the honor of God and subversive of their covenant relations with Him as His people.<div eID="gen1571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither seek after wizards--</hi>fortunetellers, who pretended, as the Hebrew word indicates, to prognosticate by palmistry (or an inspection of the lines of the hand) the future fate of those who applied to them. <div eID="gen1572" type="x-p"/>
entries.e40c1cb523f8a33232ed26e10c52ad59346c54cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1145"/><div sID="gen1573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1145"/><hi type="bold">33-34. if a stranger sojourn with thee in your land, ye shall not vex him--</hi>The Israelites were to hold out encouragement to strangers to settle among them, that they might be brought to the knowledge and worship of the true God; and with this in view, they were enjoined to treat them not as aliens, but as friends, on the ground that they themselves, who were strangers in Egypt, were at first kindly and hospitably received in that country. <div eID="gen1573" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce20a6833a68fae5e179838f8614909474043dfb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1146"/><div sID="gen1574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1146"/><hi type="bold">37. I am the Lord--</hi>This solemn admonition, by which these various precepts are repeatedly sanctioned, is equivalent to "I, your Creator--your Deliverer from bondage, and your Sovereign, who have wisdom to establish laws, have power also to punish the violation of them." It was well fitted to impress the minds of the Israelites with a sense of their duty and God's claims to obedience. <chapter eID="Lev.19"/>

entries.4ea7c3b2bd2356ef9e970f02e18453a970c7ecfa: <div eID="gen4823" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4824" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4825" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4825" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4824" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4826" type="x-p"/> Exhortations to holiness, and a repetition of various laws, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.1">Lev 19:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.2">Lev 19:2</reference> Duty to parents, and observance of the Sabbath, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.3">Lev 19:3</reference>. Against idolatry, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.4">Lev 19:4</reference>. Concerning peace-offerings, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.5-Lev.19.8">Lev 19:5-8</reference>. The gleanings of the harvest and vintage to be left for the poor, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.9">Lev 19:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.10">Lev 19:10</reference>. Against stealing and lying, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.11">Lev 19:11</reference>; false swearing, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.12">Lev 19:12</reference>; defrauding the hireling, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.13">Lev 19:13</reference>. Laws in behalf of the deaf and the blind, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.14">Lev 19:14</reference>. Against respect of persons in judgment, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.15">Lev 19:15</reference>; tale-bearing, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.16">Lev 19:16</reference>; hatred and uncharitableness, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">Lev 19:17</reference>; revenge, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">Lev 19:18</reference>; unlawful mixtures in cattle, seed, and garments, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.19">Lev 19:19</reference>. Laws relative to the bondmaid that is betrothed, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.20-Lev.19.22">Lev 19:20-22</reference>. The fruit of the trees of the land not to be eaten for the first three years, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.23">Lev 19:23</reference>; but this is lawful in the fourth and fifth years, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.24">Lev 19:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.25">Lev 19:25</reference>. Against eating of blood, and using incantations, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.26">Lev 19:26</reference>; superstitious cutting of the hair, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.27">Lev 19:27</reference>; and cutting of the flesh in the times of mourning, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.28">Lev 19:28</reference>; prostitution, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.29">Lev 19:29</reference>. Sabbaths to be reverenced, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.30">Lev 19:30</reference>. Against consulting those who are wizards, and have familiar spirits, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference>. Respect must be shown to the aged, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.32">Lev 19:32</reference>. The stranger shall not be oppressed, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.33">Lev 19:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.34">Lev 19:34</reference>. They shall keep just measures, weights, and balances, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.35">Lev 19:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.36">Lev 19:36</reference>. Conclusion, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.37">Lev 19:37</reference>.
entries.ce6de3c45756108e54b3de8b599d35c0c723ff69: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen4826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4827" type="x-p"/> Ye shall fear every man his mother, etc. - Ye shall have the profoundest reverence and respect for them. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.48.12">Gen 48:12</reference>, and see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.20.8">Exo 20:8</reference>, and see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.20.12">Exo 20:12</reference>.
entries.795ab54ce435793efe699e4927b24a6a2c53d8ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen4827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4828" type="x-p"/> Turn ye not unto idols - אלילם elilim, literally nothings; and to this St. Paul seems to allude <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.4">1Cor 8:4</reference>, where he says, We know that an idol is Nothing in the world.
entries.021be6848c55f521a0c99de91b93ee5c40e3d49f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen4828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4829" type="x-p"/> Peace-offerings - See the notes at the conclusion of Leviticus 7 at <reference osisRef="Lev.7.38">Lev 7:38</reference> (note).
entries.a7127594fb3593065e69db7fb5b04c162876125f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen4829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4830" type="x-p"/> It is be eaten - on the third day - See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.7.15">Lev 7:15</reference>.
entries.325e6deb38b35febb5ebfaae33fc3508e523f342: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen4830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4831" type="x-p"/> When ye reap the harvest - Liberty for the poor to glean both the corn-fields and vineyards was a Divine institution among the Jews; for the whole of the Mosaic dispensation, like the Christian, breathed love to God and benevolence to man. The poor in Judea were to live by gleanings from the corn-fields and vine yards. To the honor of the public and charitable spirit of the English, this merciful law is in general as much attended to as if it had been incorporated with the Gospel.
entries.d60941c7586c1527b851630ab770058a35d595f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen4831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4832" type="x-p"/> Ye shall not steal, etc. - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.20.15">Exo 20:15</reference>.
entries.a39eadf4521046e10e9f00ca38a19adb81a411a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen4832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4833" type="x-p"/> The wages - shall not abide with thee all night - For this plain reason, it is the support of the man's life and family, and they need to expend it as fast as it is earned.
entries.170a58db86d26ac8399205d80ec9b6ce76d2a33e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen4833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4834" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not curse the deaf - Or speak evil of him, because he cannot hear, and so cannot vindicate his own character. <div eID="gen4834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4835" type="x-p"/> Nor put a stumbling - block before the blind - He who is capable of doing this, must have a heart cased with cruelty. The spirit and design of these precepts are, that no man shall in any case take advantage of the ignorance, simplicity, or inexperience of his neighbor, but in all things do to his neighbor as he would, on a change of circumstances, that his neighbor should do to him.
entries.167ff825fe693ca8b5d9853ac4f6388f373c7a5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen4835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4836" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not go up and down as a tale-bearer - רכיל rachil signifies a trader, a peddler, and is here applied to the person who travels about dealing in scandal and calumny, getting the secrets of every person and family, and retailing them wherever he goes. A more despicable character exists not: such a person is a pest to society, and should be exiled from the habitations of men. <div eID="gen4836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4837" type="x-p"/> Neither shalt thou stand against the blood, etc. - Thou shalt not be as a false witness, because by such testimony the blood - the life of an innocent man may be endangered.
entries.9ff68cb7f0012f3bf8e4d69584d2bd209fa1c63c: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen4837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4838" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not hate thy brother - Thou shalt not only not do him any kind of evil, but thou shalt harbor no hatred in thy heart towards him. On the contrary, thou shalt love him as thyself, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">Lev 19:18</reference>. Many persons suppose, from misunderstanding our Lord's words, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.34">Joh 13:34</reference>, A new commandment give I unto you, that ye love one another, etc., that loving our neighbor as ourselves was first instituted under the Gospel. This verse shows the opinion to be unfounded: but to love another as Christ has loved us, i. e., to lay down our lives for each other, is certainly a new commandment; we have it simply on the authority of Jesus Christ alone. <div eID="gen4838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4839" type="x-p"/> And not suffer sin upon him - If thou see him sin, or know him to be addicted to any thing by which the safety of his soul is endangered, thou shalt mildly and affectionately reprove him, and by no means permit him to go on without counsel and advice in a way that is leading him to perdition. In a multitude of cases timely reproof has been the means of saving the soul. Speak to him privately if possible; if not, write to him in such a way that himself alone shall see it.
entries.b0aa6c52c6f55b6e7e16f64295424777183c0470: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen4839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4840" type="x-p"/> Gender with a diverse kind - These precepts taken literally seem to imply that they should not permit the horse and the she-ass, nor the he-ass and the cow, (as they do in the East), to couple together; nor sow different kinds of seeds in the same field or garden; nor have garments of silk and woolen, cotton and silk, linen and wool, etc. And if all these were forbidden, there must have been some moral reason for the prohibitions, because domestic economy required several of these mixtures, especially those which relate to seeds and clothing. With respect to heterogeneous mixtures among cattle, there is something very unnatural in it, and it was probably forbidden to prevent excitements to such unnatural lusts as those condemned in the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.22">Lev 18:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.23">Lev 18:23</reference>. As to seeds, in many cases it would be very improper to sow different kinds in the same plot of ground. It would be improvident to sow oats and wheat together: the latter would be injured, the former ruined. The turnip and carrot would not succeed conjointly, where either of them separately would prosper and yield a good crop; so we may say of many other kinds of seeds; and if this be all that is intended, the counsels are prudential agricultural maxims. As to different kinds of garments, such as the linsey woolsey, the prohibition here might be intended as much against pride and vanity as any thing else; for it is certain that both these articles may be so manufactured in conjunction as to minister to pride, though in general the linsey woolsey or drugget is the clothing of the poor. But we really do not know what the original word שעטנז shaatnez, which we translate linen and woolen, means: it is true that in <reference osisRef="Deu.22.11">Deu 22:11</reference>, where it is again used, it seems to be explained by the words immediately following, Thou shalt not wear a garment of divers sorts, as of linen and woolen together; but this may as well refer to a garment made up of a sort of patchwork differently colored and arranged for pride and for show. A folly of this kind prevailed anciently in this very land, and I shall give a proof of it, taken from a sermon against luxury in dress, composed in the fourteenth century. "As to the first sinne in superfluitie of clothing, soche that maketh it so dere, to the harme of the peple, nat only the cost of enbrauderlng, the disguised endenting, or barring, ounding paling, winding or bending and semblable wast of clothe in vanite. But there is also the costlewe furring in their gounes, so moche pounsing of chesel, to make holes; so moche dagging with sheres foorth; with the superfluitie in length of the forsaied gounes, - to grete dammage of pore folke - And more ouer - they shewe throughe disguising, in departing of ther hosen in white and red, semeth that halfe ther members were slain - They departe ther hosen into other colors, as is white and blewe, or white and blacke, or blacke and red, and so forth; than semeth it as by variaunce of color, that the halfe part of ther members ben corrupt by the fire of Saint Anthony, or by canker, or other suche mischaunce." <div eID="gen4840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4841" type="x-p"/> The Parson's Tale, in Chaucer, p. 198. Urry's edit. <div eID="gen4841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4842" type="x-p"/> The reader will pardon the antiquated spelling. "What could exhibit," says Dr. Henry, "a more fantastical appearance than an English beau of the 14th century? He wore long pointed shoes, fastened to his knees by gold or silver chains; hose of one color on the one leg, and of another color on the other; short breeches which did reach to the middle of his thighs; a coat the one half white, the other half black or blue; a long beard; a silk hood buttoned under his chin, embroidered with grotesque figures of animals, dancing men, etc., and sometimes ornamented with gold and precious stones." This dress was the height of the mode in the reign of King Edward III. Something of the same kind seems to have existed in the patriarchal times; witness the coat of many colors made by Jacob for his son Joseph. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.37.3">Gen 37:3</reference>. Concerning these different mixtures much may be seen in the Mishna, Tract, Kilaim, and in Ainsworth, and Calmet on this place.
entries.41c621d55c0149d57ead4f0e8d5e08dfd6677580: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen4842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4843" type="x-p"/> A woman that is a bondmaid - Had she been free, the law required that she should be put to death; (see <reference osisRef="Deu.22.24">Deu 22:24</reference>); but as she was a slave, she is supposed to have less self-command, and therefore less guilt: but as it is taken for granted she did not make resistance, or did consent, she is to be scourged, and the man is to bring a ram for a trespass-offering.
entries.7a220029f77188d993c167f7c413d123c7442aee: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen4843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4844" type="x-p"/> Three years shall it be as uncircumcised - I see no great reason to seek for mystical meanings in this prohibition. The fruit of a young tree cannot be good; for not having arrived at a state of maturity, the juices cannot be sufficiently elaborated to produce fruit excellent in its kind.
